title: Why You Shouldn’t Correct Student Work
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case that correcting daily independent work is largely wasted teacher time, since students rarely look at returned work and parents pay attention only to grades and report cards, not day-to-day corrections. He reframes independent work as practice rather than as material that needs to be scrutinized: its purpose is to groove memory and build automaticity on top of what a teacher has already taught in detail, not to serve as a new learning event. Under his 'better way,' teachers still check that homework is complete and glance over work to confirm students are on track, but reserve real grading and correction for tests, projects, essays, and presentations. He argues this approach saves teachers hours while also building a growth mindset and stronger performance, since students learn to work through mistakes on their own before being formally assessed.
points: Students and parents rarely look closely at corrected daily work, making hours of correction largely wasted effort.
Treat independent work as practice that grooves memory and skill, not as new material requiring correction.
Still check that homework is complete and glance at work for understanding, without correcting every item.
Reserve real grading and scrutiny for tests, projects, essays, and presentations that follow the practice period.
This approach saves significant teacher time while building growth mindset and higher student performance.
quotes: One of the worst kept secrets in teaching is that students don’t pay any attention to returned work. They may glance at the grade—if you leave one—but then they’ll stuff it in their backpack to throw away later.
Because few students actually show it to them, most parents will never see day-to-day corrected work. Those that do, that even know it exists, are too busy to go over it with their child.

The purpose of independent work isn’t to learn in its strictest sense. It’s to practice. It’s to groove the memory. It’s to sharpen the skill and make it second nature so they can build on its base the next day.
This approach is not only easier on you, and a remarkable time-saver, but it also results in greater performance and higher grades for them.
Or, better yet, have your students do it themselves as a daily reminder that practice and repetition is the pathway to knowledge, skill, and, ultimately, success.
